sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: x] be the measure of [MATH: \angle{A}.] Then [MATH: m\angle {C}=3x.]

Since the sum of the interior angles is [MATH: 180^{\circ}], we have [MATH: m∠A + m∠B + m∠C|= 180^{∘}; x + 20^{∘} + 3x|= 180^{∘}; 4x + 20^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 4x|= 160^{∘}; x|= 40^{∘}.]

Therefore, [MATH: m\angle{A}=40^{\circ}] and [MATH: m\angle {C}=3 \cdot 40^\circ = 120^{\circ}.]

So, [MATH: ABC] is an obtuse triangle because it has an obtuse angle ([MATH: m\angle {C} > 90^{\circ}]).

Content:
Consider the following scalene triangle, where [MATH: AB=5], [MATH: BC=7,] and [MATH: AC=6] units, respectively.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3f4cf679864847a6e1ab87ec203b6bb5]

Content:
Looking at the angles, it's hard to tell which angle is the largest.

Content:
However, since we know the sides, there is a simple rule that we can use to determine the relative size of the angles:

Content:
> Longer sides are opposite to larger angles and vice versa.

Content:
Applying this rule to [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] depicted above, the longest side is [MATH: \overline{BC}.] Therefore, the largest angle is the angle opposite to [MATH: \overline{BC},] which is [MATH: \color{red}\angle{A}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8a37a79a269eba01d8712387f2e9058b]

Content:
Similarly,

Content:
- the mid-sized side ([MATH: \overline{AC}]) is opposite to the mid-sized angle ([MATH: \angle B]), and
- the shortest side ([MATH: \overline{AB}]) is opposite to the smallest angle ([MATH: \angle C]).

Content:
So, from least to greatest, the angles of the triangle are ordered as follows:
[MATH: m\angle{C} < m\angle{B} < m\angle{A}]

Content:
Note: This rule works in reverse too. If you know the biggest angle of a triangle, the longest side is always opposite to this angle.

Content:

Looking at the angles, it's hard to tell which angle is the largest.

Content:
However, since we know the sides, there is a simple rule that we can use to determine the relative size of the angles:

Content:
> Longer sides are opposite to larger angles and vice versa.

Content:
Applying this rule to [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] depicted above, the longest side is [MATH: \overline{BC}.] Therefore, the largest angle is the angle opposite to [MATH: \overline{BC},] which is [MATH: \color{red}\angle{A}.]

Similarly,

Content:
- the mid-sized side ([MATH: \overline{AC}]) is opposite to the mid-sized angle ([MATH: \angle B]), and
- the shortest side ([MATH: \overline{AB}]) is opposite to the smallest angle ([MATH: \angle C]).

Content:
So, from least to greatest, the angles of the triangle are ordered as follows:
[MATH: m\angle{C} < m\angle{B} < m\angle{A}]

Content:
Note: This rule works in reverse too. If you know the biggest angle of a triangle, the longest side is always opposite to this angle.
